Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text), same article

entry.evidence: It is therefore challenging to determine the formation mechanisms of rhizoliths, which form in different sedimentary and diagenetic environments

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text (jats_text) with PDF for figure pages

steps.action: The authors frame rhizolith formation mechanisms as an open question, citing the many factors in the literature that can affect formation.
steps.quote: It is therefore challenging to determine the formation mechanisms of rhizoliths

steps.action: The authors take from their own earlier study the horizontally preserved pristine rhizoliths of the Tengeri Desert as the only prior desert case.
steps.quote: pristine rhizoliths from deserts have only been investigated at one site (Tengeri Desert, NW China)

steps.action: The authors conjecture that vertical (Badain Jaran) and horizontal (Tengeri) pristine rhizoliths may form by different mechanisms tied to contrasting settings.
steps.quote: These two types of pristine rhizoliths – horizontal- or vertical- – might have different mechanisms of formation

steps.action: The authors locate the single place with in-situ rhizoliths, sample five sites on the desert margin, and excavate a 50 cm pit around an in-situ rhizolith.
steps.quote: IRs were only found at one place in the southeastern peripheral margin of the desert

steps.action: Field description of surface weathered rhizoliths (EWR) and vertical in-situ rhizoliths (IR), the vegetation, soil moisture with depth, and the soil class (Leptic Regosols).
steps.quote: Only five IRs were found in an area of about 20 × 20 m2 in a swale where EWRs were also present

steps.action: Thin-section petrography with Alizarin red-S staining of one IR specimen shows quartz, feldspar and lithogenic carbonate grains in micritic cement without diagenetic alteration.
steps.quote: The grains are entrapped by micritic calcareous cement with no sign of post-diagenetic alteration

steps.action: Cathodoluminescence, a second method, confirms the grain identities from optical petrography, and SEM-EDX identifies the cement as low-Mg calcite.
steps.quote: [...] analyses (Fig. 4b) confirmed the nature of the clastic grains of the rhizoliths

steps.action: AMS radiocarbon ages of the root relicts and carbonate cement of the IR and EWR are calibrated (IntCal20, per Methods §3 ¶2), giving root relicts at 2053 cal BP (IR) and modern (EWR), and cements at 8628 and 5232 cal BP.
steps.quote: The age of the EWR cement is 5232 ± 19 years cal BP and the IR cement is 8628 ± 32 years cal BP.

steps.action: δ13C and δ18O are measured on the EWR cement, the IR cement and Artemisia tissues; the IR and EWR cements are similar (about −2.5‰ δ13C).
steps.quote: Similar values were observed for the IR cement, with δ13C and δ18O values of −2.5‰ and −6.2‰.

steps.action: The measured Artemisia δ13C values are checked against the literature range for C3 plants, confirming that Artemisia is a C3 plant.
steps.quote: The δ13C values of the Artemisia tissues (−26.74‰ to −28‰, Table 2) confirm the C3 nature of Artemisia

steps.action: The authors take from the literature the expectation that rhizolith δ13C is enriched by 14 to 16‰ relative to root-derived carbon.
steps.quote: their δ13C values are generally enriched by about 14‰ to 16‰ related to the root-derived C

steps.action: The observed offset between Artemisia (about −27‰) and the rhizolith cement (about −2 to −3‰) is compared with the expectation and found to be much larger.
steps.quote: is much larger than 14−16 ‰

steps.action: Three rival explanations for the offset are stated: a C4 source plant, surface diagenesis, or a large lithogenic carbonate contribution from fast formation.
steps.quote: Logically and theoretically, there are three possible explanations for this difference

steps.action: The C4-plant rival is rejected on the field association between rhizoliths and Artemisia.
steps.quote: The first hypothesis can be rejected, as field observations clearly showed the close association between rhizoliths and Artemisia plants

steps.action: The diagenesis rival is excluded because microscopy shows no diagenetic changes in the carbonates.
steps.quote: the second one can be excluded, as microscopic analyses revealed no diagenetic changes in the rhizoliths carbonates

steps.action: The surviving lithogenic-contribution explanation is checked against a second line of evidence, the radiocarbon age gap between root relicts and cement.
steps.quote: also supported by a large age discrepancy between root remains and the rhizolith cement (Table 1)

steps.action: The authors keep the lithogenic carbonate contribution as the most likely explanation of the δ13C enrichment.
steps.quote: Therefore, the third hypothesis is the most [...]

steps.action: Using cited desert studies (Mojave, central Iran), the claim is refined to add atmospheric CO2 infiltration under sparse vegetation as an enhancing factor.
steps.quote: lead to infiltration of atmospheric CO2 and can further enhance this enrichment

steps.action: Soil paleotemperatures are estimated from the cement δ18O with the Holocene empirical equation of Dworkin et al. (2005) (Methods §3 ¶3-5).
steps.quote: we applied an empirical model for paleotemperature reconstruction based on Holocene carbonates

steps.action: The reconstructed temperatures are compared with the recorded modern mean annual temperature and found to be 2 to 3 °C higher.
steps.quote: ca. 2 to 3 °C higher than the mean annual temperature recorded in the region

steps.action: The authors take from their earlier study the estimate that more than 90% of the rhizolith carbonate is lithogenic.
steps.quote: the analyzed rhizoliths consist of a large contribution (more than 90%) of lithogenic carbonates from our pre-studies

steps.action: On that inherited fraction, the authors judge rhizolith-based paleoenvironmental reconstructions for the desert unreliable, even though the temperatures look reasonable.
steps.quote: challenges the reliability of any paleo-environmental reconstructions based on rhizoliths for Badain Jaran desert

steps.action: Two potential Ca2+ sources are proposed, lithogenic carbonate dissolution and feldspar weathering; neither is tested against the other.
steps.quote: There are two potential sources of Ca2+ for calcification of the initial intact rhizoliths in the Badain Jaran desert

steps.action: A mechanism is built: fast calcification over a few drying events after root death traps lithogenic carbonate, which makes these rhizoliths unsuitable for paleo-reconstruction and dating.
steps.quote: rhizoliths form relatively fast, over a few drying events, and even after root death

steps.action: Field context and cited work are combined into a conceptual model (Fig. 5) of a semi-closed weak redox subsoil with moisture supplied by topographic position.
steps.quote: Rhizolith formation around decaying roots needs a semi-closed, weak redox environment

steps.action: A taphonomic sequence is proposed in which IRs are eroded out and thinned into EWRs, with root hairs preserved by aridity and the cement.
steps.quote: IRs are progressively eroded out of dune soils and become thinner due to wind and weathering, forming the EWRs

steps.action: The authors conclude with four controlling factors (Artemisia vegetation, soil moisture, topographic position, aridity) and fast formation incorporating old lithogenic carbon.
steps.quote: The in-situ rhizoliths are shown to be formed over a very short time after root death

No; formation is inferred from traces (morphology, isotopes, 14C)
Explain the formation mechanism and environmental conditions
Three rivals for the δ13C offset (C4 plant, diagenesis, lithogenic carbonate); two Ca sources
Partly: rivals differ in plant association and diagenetic texture; Ca sources not distinguished
Conditions found in the field at one site, not set

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Weakly: five IRs at one place, one specimen examined in detail, one 14C date per type
Limited: CL confirms petrography; 14C age gap supports the kept rival; no sensitivity tests
Lithogenic carbonate contribution from fast formation is the most likely explanation

end.claim: Intact in-situ rhizoliths of the Badain Jaran Desert formed quickly around dead Artemisia roots in moist, semi-closed redox swale subsoils, trapping lithogenic carbonate that explains their enriched δ13C and the 14C age gap between cement and root relicts.

decisive_move.sentence: Radiocarbon dating of both the root relicts and the carbonate cement of the same rhizoliths produced the age discrepancy that supports the lithogenic-carbonate explanation and the fast-formation claim.

gates.evidence: Sampling followed the discovery of the in-situ rhizoliths at one site (§3 ¶1). The horizontal-versus-vertical conjecture (§1 ¶4) motivated the study but was never tested. Two rivals were exposed to checks that could have failed (field association, microscopy, §5.1 ¶3); the kept rival was supported only by consistency with the 14C age gap. Nothing was fixed before the data.

imports.item: SEM with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy

novelty_claims.quote: To date, pristine rhizoliths from deserts have only been investigated at one site (Tengeri Desert, NW China)
but rarely in-situ in their initial states buried under the soil of desert in the Badain Jaran Desert

limits:
1. The more-than-90% lithogenic carbon fraction, given as a result in the abstract, is inherited from the authors' earlier study (Sun et al. 2019a) and was not measured here (§5.1 ¶4).
2. Sample sizes are very small: one IR specimen for petrography, one 14C date per material and type, and two IR isotope analyses, both from position G and likely the same rhizolith (inference from Table 2).
3. The abstract claims the root relicts belong to Artemisia; no species identification of the relicts is reported, only co-occurrence and the C3 δ13C of living plants (inference).
4. Soil moisture, redox state and Ca2+ were not measured; the semi-closed redox model (Fig. 5) rests on field moisture description and cited work.
5. The two Ca sources are not distinguished by any test.
6. The horizontal-versus-vertical contrast with the Tengeri rhizoliths, stated as motivation, is not tested or discussed later.
7. The Methods state IntCal20 calibration, while the Table 1 note says CALIB7.1/CALIBomb.
8. The conclusion calls the roots 'modern dead roots', yet the IR relict dates to 2053 cal BP.
9. Holocene formation (8 to 2 ka) is inferred from apparent carbonate ages that the paper itself deems unreliable for dating.
10. Sub-claims and their statuses: the paleotemperature estimate is not kept (judged unreliable, status none); the controlling-factor list in §6 is best_explanation, without rivals tested.

disagreements.target: Recently published works suggesting rhizoliths suit paleoenvironmental reconstruction (Gocke et al. 2010, 2011, 2014; Bojanowski et al. 2015; Li et [...]
disagreements.support: Fast formation and incomplete recrystallization, inferred from the 14C age gap and δ13C enrichment, make these specific rhizoliths unsuitable for reconstruction and dating.
disagreements.quote: This is in contrast with many recently published works that suggest the suitability of rhizoliths [...]

disagreements.target: Expected 14–16‰ δ13C enrichment of rhizoliths over root-derived C (Cerling 1984; Cerling and Quade 1993; Zamanian et [...] )
disagreements.support: The measured offset between Artemisia tissue and cement is much larger, which the authors attribute to lithogenic carbonate rather than to a failure of the equilibrium model.

disagreements.target: Paleotemperature reconstruction from pedogenic carbonate δ18O (Dworkin et al. 2005 equation) applied to rhizoliths
disagreements.support: The reconstructed temperatures are 2–3 °C above recorded values, and the inherited lithogenic fraction makes such reconstructions unreliable for this desert.
disagreements.quote: challenges the reliability of any paleo-environmental reconstructions based on rhizoliths for Badain Jaran desert

alternatives_considered.chosen: Large lithogenic carbonate contribution due to fast rhizolith formation
alternatives_considered.alternatives: C4 source plant other than Artemisia; diagenetic alteration at the soil surface
alternatives_considered.reason: Field association with Artemisia rejects the C4 rival; microscopy shows no diagenesis; the 14C age gap supports the third

alternatives_considered.chosen: Vertical buried rhizoliths treated as pristine in-situ rhizoliths (IR)
alternatives_considered.reason: Only the vertical rhizoliths preserved in sand soil were expected to be pristine
